content: Nucleic acids are macromolecules composed of chains of nucleotides. In biochemistry, these molecules serve as carriers of genetic information or form structural components within cells. The two most common types of nucleic acids are deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA). Nucleic acids are universally present in all living organisms, as they are found in every cell. They are also present in viruses. Artificial nucleic acids, such as peptide nucleic acid (PNA), morpholino, locked nucleic acid (LNA), glycol nucleic acid (GNA), and threose nucleic acid (TNA), differ from naturally occurring DNA or RNA due to modifications in their molecular backbones. The term nucleic acid refers to a family of biopolymers named for their role in the cell nucleus. Nucleic acids are constructed from monomers called nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of three components: a nitrogenous heterocyclic base (either a purine or a pyrimidine), a pentose sugar, and a phosphate group. DNA and RNA differ in the structure of the sugar in their nucleotides—DNA contains 2-deoxyribose, while RNA contains ribose. Additionally, the nitrogenous bases differ between the two types: adenine, cytosine, and guanine are found in both DNA and RNA, but thymine is exclusive to DNA, and uracil is exclusive to RNA. Rare nucleic acid bases, such as inosine, can also occur, for example, in mature transfer RNA (tRNA) strands. Nucleic acids can be single-stranded or double-stranded, though structures with three or more strands can also form. Double-stranded nucleic acids, such as the DNA double helix, consist of two single-stranded nucleic acids held together by hydrogen bonds. In contrast, RNA is typically single-stranded, but individual RNA strands can fold back on themselves to form secondary structures, as seen in tRNA and ribosomal RNA (rRNA). Within cells, DNA is usually double-stranded, although some viruses have single-stranded DNA genomes. Retroviruses, on the other hand, have single-stranded RNA genomes. The sugars and phosphates in nucleic acids are connected in an alternating chain via shared oxygen atoms, forming a phosphodiester functional group. This arrangement gives nucleic acids polarity, with the phosphate groups attaching to the 3' and 5' carbons of the sugar. The nitrogenous bases extend from a glycosidic linkage to the 1' carbon of the pentose sugar ring. Bases are joined through the N-1 position of pyrimidines and the N-9 position of purines to the 1' carbon of ribose via an N-β glycosyl bond. RNA, or ribonucleic acid, is a nucleic acid polymer composed of nucleotide monomers. It plays several critical roles in translating genetic information from DNA into proteins. RNA acts as a messenger between DNA and ribosomes, the protein synthesis complexes. It also forms essential components of ribosomes and serves as a carrier molecule for amino acids during protein synthesis. DNA, or deoxyribonucleic acid, is a nucleic acid that contains the genetic instructions necessary for the development and functioning of all known living organisms. The primary role of DNA is the long-term storage of genetic information. DNA is often compared to a set of blueprints, as it contains the instructions required to construct other cellular components, such as proteins and RNA molecules. The segments of DNA that carry genetic information are called genes, while other DNA sequences serve structural purposes or regulate the use of genetic information. Nucleobases are heterocyclic aromatic organic compounds containing nitrogen atoms. They are the components of RNA and DNA involved in base pairing. Cytosine, guanine, adenine, and thymine are predominantly found in DNA, while uracil replaces thymine in RNA. These bases are abbreviated as C, G, A, T, and U, respectively. Nucleobases are complementary and pair specifically: cytosine pairs with guanine, and adenine pairs with thymine (or uracil in RNA). The interaction between cytosine and guanine is stronger than that between adenine and thymine because the former pair is joined by three hydrogen bonds, while the latter pair has only two. Consequently, DNA molecules with higher guanine-cytosine (GC) content are more stable and have higher melting temperatures. Nucleobases are classified into two main groups based on their molecular skeletons: double-ringed purines (adenine and guanine) and single-ringed pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, and uracil). Mutant forms of adenine and guanine, such as hypoxanthine and xanthine, can arise through mutagenic processes like deamination, where an amine group is replaced with a hydroxyl group. These are abbreviated as HX and X, respectively. Nucleosides are glycosylamines formed by attaching a nucleobase to a ribose or deoxyribose sugar ring. In essence, a nucleoside is a base linked to a sugar. The names of nucleosides are derived from the names of their corresponding nucleobases. Common nucleosides in DNA and RNA include cytidine, uridine, adenosine, guanosine, and thymidine. When a phosphate group is added to a nucleoside (via phosphorylation by a specific kinase enzyme), a nucleotide is formed. Nucleoside analogues, such as acyclovir, are used as antiviral agents. A nucleotide consists of a nucleoside and one or more phosphate groups. Nucleotides are the monomers of RNA and DNA and also serve as structural units of several important cofactors, such as coenzyme A (CoA), flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), flavin mononucleotide (FMN), adenosine triphosphate (ATP), and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP). In cells, nucleotides play critical roles in metabolism and signaling. Nucleotides are named based on the nucleoside they are derived from and the number of phosphate groups they contain. For example, adenine bonded to ribose forms the nucleoside adenosine. When adenosine is bonded to a phosphate group, it forms adenosine monophosphate (AMP). As additional phosphate groups are added, adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) are formed sequentially.
